title: Choose the visual world for mufasil.site
question: Fresh hand, steered to professional and creative. The roll assigned Release Notes. Keep it, take my pick or an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Release Notes
options.lineage: the changelogs engineers and CTOs read every week
options.thesis: His career published as release notes: every role a version, every result an entry.
options.viewport: The current release, v12 at Social Champ, set at poster scale with its entries; Download CV and Start a project sit in the release header like the install command.
options.risk: If the type is timid it becomes an ordinary timeline; it lives or dies on scale and typographic discipline.

raised.raise: Every block is reduced to the one job it does; nothing on the page is decoration without a fact.
One focal release at the centre of the first viewport, with every earlier version radiating down from it.
A single vertical axis: the eye runs one line from the current role to the first job in 2014.
Relationships are drawn: each release links visibly to its case study and its write-up.

options.label: Annual Report
options.lineage: the printed annual reports boards and investors read
options.thesis: Eleven years reported like a company: key figures, a letter, segment reviews, an outlook.
options.viewport: A report cover with key figures set huge (11+ years, 19+ engineers, 4 months), a short signed letter, and Download CV as the report download.
options.risk: Familiar to anyone who has read a corporate report, and it can turn stiff if the letter reads like marketing.

options.label: Expedition Newspaper
options.lineage: a newspaper hand-set and printed in a polar winter hut
options.thesis: A one-man newspaper reporting each shipped project as front-page news.
materials: one black ink on rag paper
options.viewport: A masthead, the lead story on the delayed product shipped in four months, and issue numbers as navigation.
options.case: Recruiters read a front page instantly, so clarity holds; the rough hand-printed finish fights the professional brief.
options.risk: The newspaper portfolio is a known trope, and rough print can read unpolished.

options.label: Bauhaus Workshop
options.thesis: Primary shapes on a white table as building blocks.
options.viewport: Circle, square and triangle arranged around his name.
options.case: Creative, but nothing in it says backend or senior engineer.
options.kept: Reduce every element to the one job it does.

options.label: Patch Bay Schedule
options.thesis: Skills wired to their defaults with amber link lines.
options.viewport: Numbered lanes linking roles to skills.
options.case: Engineers get it; recruiters will not.
options.risk: A control surface where a person should be.
options.kept: Draw relationships instead of describing them.

options.label: Collider Event Display
options.thesis: One collision, every track a career path.
options.viewport: Tracks curving out of his name into roles.
options.case: Beautiful, but the metaphor needs explaining.
options.kept: One frozen focal moment, everything radiating from it.

options.label: Living Skin
options.thesis: A surface that changes pattern to signal state.
options.viewport: A rippling field behind his name.
options.case: No tie to his work and hard to make professional.
options.kept: The surface itself signals state, such as availability.

options.label: Garden Vistas
options.thesis: A career laid out as axial vistas and hidden rooms.
options.viewport: A long avenue leading to his name.
options.case: Grand, but it says royalty, not engineering.
options.kept: One long central axis that leads the eye to the action.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A dark developer portfolio, executed with care.
canonCard.viewport: Name and role beside a photo, an availability badge, a CV button and a row of stats.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from hundreds of developer portfolios by design.
